transcript: and Arizona, the Republican candidate's election was flawed. You know, William F. Buckley, the late conservative writer and columnist, used to say, Republicans should nominate the most conservative candidate who can win the general election. Well, in the year of Trump, we're particularly seeing Republican primary voters nominate candidates in the primary who cannot win the general election. And it's a lesson that has been learned repeatedly, but somehow a lot of people don't get the message. The House, it was very similar. In each of the cases, a number of cases I can point to where Republicans nominated a candidate who may have satisfied the Trump wing of the Republican Party, but who simply weren't going to be able to win. The Trump endorsement, let's be frank, is very, very good in a lot of the very red states. Very important, you saw Liz Cheney lost her primary by 30 points. in Alabama and Mississippi and Texas and a number of other states, that Trump endorsement is very helpful to those candidates. But if you look up and down the line in states and districts that are swing districts that are more purple states, they're not ruby red, they're not deep blue states, the candidates with the Trump backing in those swing districts and states generally didn't win. You hear in New York, Congressman Lee Zeldin, a good friend of mine was the candidate. He was supported by President Trump, and unlike some of these other states, he made the governor's race in New York a very, very tight competitive race, because rather than running on extraneous issues, he focused like a laser on crime in the economy in New York state, and he came within five points of winning the governorship, which was quite an achievement for him, and he carried in behind him No fewer than 11 Republican congressmen from New York will go to Washington next year. And that was a very significant factor in the likelihood that the Republicans are winning a narrow control of the House of Representatives, the election of 11 Republican congressmen from New York State. So I think those are the biggest factors. We've seen post-election surveys. independent-minded voters who could swing either to the Democrats or the Republicans, independent-minded voters, a big negative factor for them was whether or not Donald Trump was supporting a candidate or not. And those people who had a choice, who were expressing a concern over Trump's support for Republican candidate, close to 60% of them voted for the Democratic candidate. And so when you're in a swing district and a swing state, you have in this increasingly polarized environment where many people are not splitting their tickets, voting a party line. There's maybe 10 to 15% of the voters who are susceptible to splitting their ticket and voting more independently of the party. And those folks are reacting very negatively to a Trump endorsement. So it's a factor and I think Republicans need to take that lesson. Democrats, I think the lesson they need to take is, and they're going to have a problem in 2024 when I think 26 Democratic incumbents are seeking reelection or Democratic held seats are seeking election. That's going to be a steep hill for them to climb. And I think the public is very much interested in finding candidates who are willing to solve problems and not simply go into their partisan corner, but actually solve problems that the country is facing. So I think there are lessons for both parties to be taken from Tuesday's result, which is going to leave us basically with a very narrow Republican majority, replacing that very narrow Democratic majority in the House, and either a 50-50 Senate or a 51-49 Senate on either side. So it's going to be very close. The question is how much can get done in the next two years with that close division in Congress?
